And secure against length extension, unlike SHA-2. - **Highly parallelizable** across any number of threads and SIMD lanes, because it's a Merkle tree on the inside. - Capable of **verified streaming** and **incremental updates**, again because it's a Merkle tree. - A **PRF**, **MAC**, **KDF**, and **XOF**, as well as a regular hash. - **One algorithm with no variants**, which is fast on x86-64 and also on smaller architectures.

The default output size is 256 bits. BLAKE3 was designed by Jack O'Connor, Samuel Neves, Jean-Philippe Aumasson, and Zooko. The development of BLAKE3 was sponsored by [Electric Coin Company](https://electriccoin.co). *NOTE: BLAKE3 is not a password hashing algorithm, because it's designed to be fast, whereas password hashing should not be fast. If you hash passwords to store the hashes or if you derive keys from passwords, we recommend [Argon2](https://github.com/P-H-C/phc-winner-argon2).* ## The `b3sum` Command Line Tool The `b3sum` command line utility prints the BLAKE3 hashes of files or of standard input. ### Usage ``` Usage: b3sum [OPTIONS] [FILE]... Arguments: [FILE]... Files to hash, or checkfiles to check Options: --keyed Use the keyed mode, reading the 32-byte key from stdin --derive-key Use the key derivation mode, with the given context string -l, --length The number of output bytes, before hex encoding [default: 32] --seek The starting output byte offset, before hex encoding [default: 0] --num-threads The maximum number of threads to use --no-mmap Disable memory mapping --no-names Omit filenames in the output --raw Write raw output bytes to stdout, rather than hex --tag Output BSD-style checksums: BLAKE3 ([FILE]) = [HASH] -c, --check Read BLAKE3 sums from the [FILE]s and check them --quiet Skip printing OK for each checked file -h, --help Print help (see more with '--help') -V, --version Print version ``` ### Examples Hash a file: ```bash b3sum foo.txt ``` Hash multiple files: ```bash b3sum file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt ``` Hash from standard input: ```bash echo "hello world" | b3sum ``` Check hashes from a checksum file: ```bash b3sum -c checksums.txt ``` Generate a longer hash output (e.g., 64 bytes): ```bash b3sum --length 64 foo.txt ``` Use keyed hashing mode: ```bash echo "my secret key padded to 32 bytes" | b3sum --keyed foo.txt ``` Use key derivation mode: ```bash b3sum --derive-key "my-app 2024-01-01 user-id" < input_key_material.bin ``` ### Installation Prebuilt binaries are available for Linux, Windows, and macOS on the [releases page](https://github.com/BLAKE3-team/BLAKE3/releases). ## BLAKE3 Library Usage BLAKE3 is available as a library for multiple programming languages. ### Rust To use BLAKE3 from Rust code, add a dependency on the `blake3` crate: ```rust // Hash an input all at once. let hash1 = blake3::hash(b"foobarbaz"); // Hash an input incrementally. let mut hasher = blake3::Hasher::new(); hasher.update(b"foo"); hasher.update(b"bar"); hasher.update(b"baz"); let hash2 = hasher.finalize(); assert_eq!(hash1, hash2); // Extended output. OutputReader also implements Read and Seek. let mut output = [0; 1000]; let mut output_reader = hasher.finalize_xof(); output_reader.fill(&mut output); assert_eq!(hash1, output[..32]); // Print a hash as hex. println!("{}", hash1); ``` ### Keyed Hashing Mode The `keyed_hash` mode takes a 256-bit key: ```rust // MAC an input all at once. let example_key = [42u8; 32]; let mac1 = blake3::keyed_hash(&example_key, b"example input"); // MAC incrementally. let mut hasher = blake3::Hasher::new_keyed(&example_key); hasher.update(b"example input"); let mac2 = hasher.finalize(); assert_eq!(mac1, mac2); ``` ### Key Derivation Mode The `derive_key` mode takes a context string and some key material (not a password). } ``` ### Other Languages BLAKE3 implementations are available for many other programming languages including: - Go - Python - JavaScript/TypeScript (Node.js and browsers) - .NET - Java Search for "BLAKE3" in your language's package repository. ## Features - **Regular hashing**: Hash any input to produce a fixed-size digest - **Keyed hashing**: Create message authentication codes (MACs) - **Key derivation**: Derive cryptographic keys from input key material - **Extended output (XOF)**: Generate arbitrary-length outputs - **Incremental updates**: Hash data in chunks as it arrives - **Multithreading**: Parallel hashing for improved performance on large inputs - **SIMD optimization**: Hardware-accelerated hashing on supported platforms ## Security Notes The default output length is 32 bytes (256 bits), which provides 128-bit security against collision attacks. # b3sum

A command line utility for calculating [BLAKE3](https://github.com/BLAKE3-team/BLAKE3) hashes,
similar to Coreutils tools like `b2sum` or `md5sum`.

## Usage

```
Usage: b3sum [OPTIONS] [FILE]...

Arguments:
  [FILE]...  Files to hash, or checkfiles to check

Options:
      --keyed                 Use the keyed mode, reading the 32-byte key from stdin
      --derive-key <CONTEXT>  Use the key derivation mode, with the given context string
  -l, --length <LEN>          The number of output bytes, before hex encoding [default: 32]
      --seek <SEEK>           The starting output byte offset, before hex encoding [default: 0]
      --num-threads <NUM>     The maximum number of threads to use
      --no-mmap               Disable memory mapping
      --no-names              Omit filenames in the output
      --raw                   Write raw output bytes to stdout, rather than hex
      --tag                   Output BSD-style checksums: BLAKE3 ([FILE]) = [HASH]
  -c, --check                 Read BLAKE3 sums from the [FILE]s and check them
      --quiet                 Skip printing OK for each checked file
  -h, --help                  Print help (see more with '--help')
  -V, --version               Print version
```

## Examples

Hash a file:

```bash
b3sum foo.txt
```

Hash multiple files:

```bash
b3sum file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt
```

Hash from standard input:

```bash
echo "hello world" | b3sum
```

Time hashing a large file to see performance:

```bash
# Create a 1 GB file
head -c 1000000000 /dev/zero > /tmp/bigfile
# Hash it with SHA-256
time openssl sha256 /tmp/bigfile
# Hash it with BLAKE3 (notice the speed difference!)
time b3sum /tmp/bigfile
```

Check hashes from a checksum file:

```bash
b3sum -c checksums.txt
```

Generate a longer hash output (e.g., 64 bytes):

```bash
b3sum --length 64 foo.txt
```

Use keyed hashing mode (for message authentication):

```bash
echo "my-32-byte-secret-key-padded!!" | b3sum --keyed message.txt
```

Use key derivation mode:

```bash
b3sum --derive-key "myapp 2024-01-01 session-token" < key_material.bin
```

Output in BSD style format:

```bash
b3sum --tag foo.txt
# Output: BLAKE3 (foo.txt) = [hash]
```

Output raw bytes instead of hex:

```bash
b3sum --raw foo.txt > hash.bin
```

Control number of threads:

```bash
b3sum --num-threads 4 large_file.dat
```

## Installation

Prebuilt binaries are available for Linux, Windows, and macOS on the
[releases page](https://github.com/BLAKE3-team/BLAKE3/releases).

]:

    # --check parsing: feed stdout back?
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False, mode='wb') as cf:

import subprocess, tempfile, os

def run(args, stdin_bytes=None):
    p = subprocess.run(["./executable"]+args, input=stdin_bytes, capture_output=True)
    return p

# Check parsing of escaped lines: test unescaping logic
# What forms are accepted?
tmpdir = tempfile.mkdtemp()
# create file with newline in name
path_newline = os.path.join(tmpdir, "a\nb")
with open(path_newline, 'wb') as f:
    f.write(b"hello\n")
# hash it correctly
p = run([path_newline])
print("correct line", p.stdout)
# Now try variants:
# 1. unescaped? (literal newline inside line would split lines) - not valid
# 2. escaped without leading backslash? i.e., "hash  /tmp/.../a\\nb" without leading \
correct = p.stdout  # starts with \
stripped = correct[1:]  # remove leading \
print("stripped", stripped)
for content, desc in [
    (correct, "correct escaped with leading \\"),
    (stripped, "escaped but no leading \\"),
    (correct.replace(b"\\n", b"\n"), "literal newline?"),
]:
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False, mode='wb') as cf:
        cf.write(content)
        cfname=cf.name
    p2 = run(["--check", cfname])
    print(f"{desc!r} => rc={p2.returncode} out={p2.stdout!r} err={p2.stderr!r}")
    os.unlink(cfname)

    f.write(b"hello\n")

    cfname=cf.name

print(f"unescaped bs check => rc={p2.returncode} out={p2.stdout!r} err={p2.stderr!r}")
os.unlink(cfname)

import shutil
shutil.rmtree(tmpdir)

# Similarly, for escaped lines, filename's \r is represented as "\\r" (two chars), not literal \r, so no ambiguity.

For "foo\r\r\n", after splitting on \n, line is "hash  foo\r\r" (with two \r). Stripping one \r would leave "hash  foo\r" -> filename "foo\r" (with one \r literal). But since \r must be escaped, that would be invalid? But we got "foo" without \r, so stripping must be all trailing \r? Or maybe reading uses .lines() which strips \r\n and \n? In Rust, .lines() splits on \n and strips trailing \r (one). But our test shows two \r stripped, so maybe it strips all? Or maybe our file "foo\r\r\n" after reading: line = "hash  foo\r" (one \r stripped by lines()), filename = "foo\r" ??? But output was "foo", not "foo\r". Hmm.
# Wait: Could be that check parsing for GNU with escaped=False treats trailing \r as part of filename, but then filename "foo\r" contains \r which would trigger escaping? No, check output for "foo\r" would be escaped? But output was "foo" without. So not.

tmpdir = tempfile.mkdtemp()
path_cr = os.path.join(tmpdir, "foo\r")  # filename ends with \r? Actually "foo\r" is foo + CR
print(repr(path_cr))
try:
    with open(path_cr, 'wb') as f:
        f.write(b"hello\n")

    print("cr file hash", p.stdout, p.stdout.hex())
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False, mode='wb') as cf:

        cfname=cf.name
        print("checkfile", open(cfname,'rb').read(), open(cfname,'rb').read().hex())
    p2 = run(["--check", cfname])
    print("check", p2.stdout, p2.stderr, p2.returncode)
    import os as _os
    _os.unlink(cfname)
    _os.unlink(path_cr)

    print("fail", e)

import subprocess
def run(args, stdin_bytes=None):
    p=subprocess.run(["./executable"]+args, input=stdin_bytes, capture_output=True)
    return p

for args in [
    ["-ch"],

]:
    # need stdin for those that read stdin to avoid hanging? Provide b"hi" for hash mode, empty for check?
    stdin = b"hi"
    # For --help cases, stdin not needed
    if "--help" in args or "-h" in args or "-V" in args or "-c" in " ".join(args):
        # For -c without file, it reads stdin checkfile, need to provide something? Provide empty?
        stdin = b"" if "-c" in args or "--check" in args else None
        if "--help" in args or "-h" in args or "-V" in args:
            stdin = None
    p=run(args, stdin_bytes=stdin)

def run_orig(args, inp=None):
    return subprocess.run(["./executable"]+args, input=inp, capture_output=True)
def run_new(args, inp=None):
    return subprocess.run(["/tmp/executable"]+args, input=inp, capture_output=True)

import subprocess, tempfile, os
def run_orig(args, inp=None):
    return subprocess.run(["./executable"]+args, input=inp, capture_output=True)
def run_new(args, inp=None):
    return subprocess.run(["/tmp/executable"]+args, input=inp, capture_output=True)
def compare(args, inp=None):
    p1=run_orig(args,inp)
    p2=run_new(args,inp)
    ok = (p1.returncode==p2.returncode and p1.stdout==p2.stdout and p1.stderr==p2.stderr)
    print(f"{args} inp={repr(inp)[:40] if inp else None} => {'OK' if ok else 'FAIL'}")
    if not ok:
        print(" orig",p1.returncode,p1.stdout[:500],p1.stderr[:500])
        print(" new ",p2.returncode,p2.stdout[:500],p2.stderr[:500])
    return ok

import tempfile as tf
with tf.NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False, mode='wb') as f:
    f.write(b"hello\n")
    fname=f.name

    cf.write(p.stdout)
    cfname=cf.name
compare(["--check", cfname])
compare(["--check", "--quiet", cfname])
# wrong hash
with tf.NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False, mode='w') as cf2:
    cf2.write("0"*64+f"  {fname}\n")
    cfname2=cf2.name
compare(["--check", cfname2])
# tag
p2=run_orig(["--tag", fname])
print("tag",p2.stdout)
with tf.NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False, mode='wb') as cf3:
    cf3.write(p2.stdout)
    cfname3=cf3.name
compare(["--check", cfname3])
# invalid lines
for content in [b"abc  foo\n", b"\n", b"", b"xxx\n", b"8e4c"+"  foo\n"]:
    with tf.NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False, mode='wb') as cf:
        cf.write(content)
        cfn=cf.name
    p1=run_orig(["--check", cfn])
    p2=run_new(["--check", cfn])
    ok=(p1.returncode==p2.returncode and p1.stdout==p2.stdout and p1.stderr==p2.stderr)
    print(f"content {content!r} => {'OK' if ok else 'FAIL'}")
    if not ok:
        print(p1.stdout,p1.stderr,p1.returncode)
        print(p2.stdout,p2.stderr,p2.returncode)
    os.unlink(cfn)

os.unlink(fname); os.unlink(cfname); os.unlink(cfname2); os.unlink(cfname3)

def ro(a,i=None):
    p=subprocess.run(["./executable"]+a, input=i, capture_output=True)

    p=subprocess.run(["/tmp/executable"]+a, input=i, capture_output=True)
    return p
def cmp(a,i=None):
    p1=ro(a,i); p2=rn(a,i)
    ok=(p1.returncode==p2.returncode and p1.stdout==p2.stdout and p1.stderr==p2.stderr)
